design_detail: Paper published as a 'Review' by the DIMS team, describing the Dutch Drug Information and Monitoring System (DIMS) and summarizing its monitoring results from 1992 to July 2010: more than 100,000 drug samples handed in anonymously at DIMS testing facilities, where tablets were either 'recognized' at the office from their recorded features and a Marquis reagent test ('office testing') or analysed in one laboratory (thin-layer chromatography with Marquis and Dragendorff reagents, gas chromatography with nitrogen–phosphorus detection, GC–MS as tiebreaker in about 10% of samples and for uncommon substances, NMR in exceptional cases) (pp. 622–624). Results are given for tablets sold as ecstasy (composition by year, 1993–2010, Figure 5), speed powders (8,239 samples), cocaine powders, and LSD and other hallucinogens, mostly in figures without sample sizes (pp. 624–629). A narrative section describes other countries' monitoring systems and shows their results from EMCDDA and other reports (Figure 11, Table 2), with no Dutch data in Figure 11 (pp. 629–632). No search or selection methods are given for the review part. Filed as cross-sectional and appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist for the DIMS monitoring data, as the round brief directs for drug-checking data; the international part is narrative and is described, not appraised.
can_establish: How DIMS identifies drugs, including identification of tablets by appearance and colour test, and what the samples handed in to DIMS contained from 1992 to 2010: the composition of tablets sold as ecstasy by year, the purity and cutting agents of speed and cocaine powders, and the content of LSD samples.
cannot_establish: How reliable identification by logo and appearance is (the 99% figure is stated without data, p. 622) or how much content varies among tablets with the same logo; the composition of the whole Dutch market (self-selected samples; the claim that people who test resemble those who do not rests on two cited studies, pp. 623–624); or how Dutch results compare with other countries (Figure 11 has no Dutch data, and methods differ by country).

sample.recruitment: Samples handed in anonymously by people who use drugs at the DIMS network of testing facilities, mostly in prevention departments of addiction-care institutions across the Netherlands; a few institutions only receive samples and send them all to the DIMS Bureau (p. 622, The Drug Information and Monitoring System). More than 100,000 samples in 1992 to July 2010; the exact total is not given (p. 624).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: All samples handed in; cannabis products, mushrooms and doping substances are not monitored systematically (p. 624). The ecstasy composition figure covers tablets analysed in the laboratory in 1993–2010 (p. 624); whether recognized tablets enter any of the results is not stated.
sample.demographics: Not collected in this paper. From two cited studies, the authors describe people who test as mostly young men of Dutch ethnic background in paid work or study, with considerable experience of alcohol, tobacco and cannabis and less of cocaine (pp. 623–624).
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected submissions. The authors take people who test to be broadly similar to people who do not, from two cited studies (pp. 623–624), state that DIMS results are not an exact representation of the market (p. 624), and note that a testing system reaches only a fraction of all people who use or may use drugs (p. 632).

exposure.measurement: Office testing: outward features (diameter, thickness, weight, colour, groove, light or dark speckling, logo and its design) and a Marquis reagent test, looked up in an online database of tablets recently analysed in a laboratory, updated weekly by the DIMS Bureau (p. 622). Laboratory (Delta Psychiatric Hospital): thin-layer chromatography (Toxilab A) with four detection stages; GC with nitrogen–phosphorus detection to quantify main components; GC–MS as tiebreaker for discrepancies or trace amounts (about 10% of samples) and to quantify uncommon substances; GC–MS and NMR in exceptional cases (pp. 622–623).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not applicable (samples). Content as mg MDMA per tablet, percentage purity of powders, µg LSD per unit.
exposure.polysubstance: Other substances reported for ecstasy tablets (Figure 5), speed (caffeine, Figure 7), cocaine (Table 1, Figure 9) and samples sold as LSD (Figure 10).

comparison.controls: None; comparisons are between years and drug types, and narratively with other countries' published monitoring results.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not reported: numbers of samples by year and drug type behind most percentages; the contents of recognized tablets; variation of content within a logo; the validation data behind the 99% figure.

outcomes.instruments: Samples per year by type (Figure 3); share of laboratory-analysed samples by drug (Figure 4); composition of tablets sold as ecstasy by year (Figure 5); mean amphetamine and caffeine in speed powders (Figure 7); cocaine purity with and without active adulterants (Figure 9) and adulterant frequencies (Table 1); share of samples sold as LSD that contained LSD and mean LSD per unit (Figure 10) (pp. 624–629).
outcomes.validity_norms: Laboratory methods are described without validation data. The 99% reliability of the recognition list is stated without methods or data (p. 622).
outcomes.operationalization: Purity = percentage of the drug in a powder; for ecstasy, shares of tablets containing MDMA, other ecstasy-like substances or other active substances; powders without quantifiable drug are counted separately.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: one difference (cocaine purity with and without synthetic local anaesthetics) is called significant without a test, statistic or P value; everything else is descriptive.

analysis.effect_sizes: Powders, mean ± SEM: speed 30.2 ± 0.2% amphetamine (1995–2010); cocaine 56 ± 0.3% among quantifiable samples, 66.3 ± 0.7% in 1993–1999 against 54.9 ± 0.8% in 2000–2010; cocaine with synthetic local anaesthetics 44.6 ± 0.9% against 57.0 ± 0.3% without, and with other active adulterants 38.8 ± 0.4% against 62.1 ± 0.3% (pp. 627–628). Ecstasy results are shares read from figures or monthly lows quoted without denominators (pp. 624–625). No intervals or tests.
analysis.preregistration_detail: Not applicable; no methods are given for the review.
analysis.selective_reporting: Monthly lows are quoted for ecstasy (October 1997, March 2009) without monthly data or denominators; the numbers behind Figures 3–5, 7, 9 and 10 are not tabulated; the 99% reliability of recognition is a single figure without data; Figure 11 is introduced as a comparison with DIMS but contains no Dutch data.

interpretation_gap.results_show: DIMS identified on average 30% of tablets by appearance and colour test against a weekly updated list of recently analysed tablets; tablets sold as ecstasy contained MDMA much less often around 1997 and 2009 than in 2000–2004; tablets resembling ecstasy, with similar logos, sometimes contained 2C-B or amphetamine instead; speed and cocaine powders varied widely in purity and cutting agents; LSD per unit varied from 1 to 500 µg.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The review says office testing gives an immediate and accurate result and that validation has shown 99% reliability of the recognition list (p. 622), without data. From two cited studies it treats the people who test as a reasonable reflection of all people who use drugs recreationally (pp. 623–624), although it later notes that a testing system reaches only a fraction of them (p. 632), and it says, citing Vogels et al. (2009), that a comparison with police seizures showed DIMS gives a fairly accurate picture of the total Dutch ecstasy market at consumer level (p. 624); that comparison relied largely on matching seized tablets to the DIMS database (card sc_vogels_2009). Figure 11 is introduced as a comparison of other countries' results with those of DIMS (p. 630) but shows no Dutch data. A typical ecstasy tablet is said to contain 80–100 mg MDMA (p. 624), without a source and above the yearly medians the same group reported from its own laboratory data (Vogels et al., 2009).

timeline.event: Vogels et al. (2009): DIMS ecstasy results for 1993–2008 and the comparison with seized tablets, cited here for the fairly accurate picture of the market (ref. 11); it gives the same 99% reliability figure without data.
Vrolijk et al. (2017, online 2016) cite this paper for the DIMS database used as the reference for online pill reports (ref. 12).
Brunt et al. (2017, TEDI) cite this paper and Vogels et al. (2009) for the reliability of DIMS tablet recognition (card sc_brunt_2017).

replication.where_it_stands: A descriptive review of a monitoring system by its own team. The reliability of identifying tablets by appearance, stated here and in Vogels et al. (2009), has no published data in either paper.

funding.funder: No funding statement in the article. The abstract says the Dutch Ministry of Health has made drug testing for people who use drugs possible since the 1990s (p. 621).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors work for DIMS at the Trimbos Institute (p. 621), the system reviewed, and the discussion argues for drug monitoring and testing (pp. 630–632). A flag for closer reading, not a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: Publication of the recognition list's validation data and of the number of tablets identified by recognition each year: for every recognized tablet later analysed in the laboratory, whether the main substance and the MDMA amount (within a stated margin) matched the batch record, with the spread of MDMA content within each logo.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Samples submitted to a national drug-checking network: a frame for what people choose to have tested, not for the market.
Self-selected submissions; similarity to people who do not test is inferred from two cited studies.
More than 100,000 samples overall and 8,239 speed powders, but the yearly denominators behind the ecstasy, cocaine and LSD percentages are not given (samples sold as LSD numbered 6 to 99 a year).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Procedures and laboratory methods are described in detail; who submits is described only from cited studies.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Whether recognized tablets enter any result is not stated, and Figure 3's category of samples 'not analyzed' is not explained.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: Laboratory identification by three techniques, with GC–MS or NMR where needed; the ecstasy composition is said to come from laboratory analysis.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way across participants
domains.note: One laboratory; whether methods or detection limits changed over 18 years is not stated.
Descriptive figures without denominators or intervals; monthly lows quoted without data; one difference called significant without a test; overlapping periods in the text on MDMA content.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low rate managed

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Single-laboratory monitoring data, appropriate for describing what samples handed in to DIMS contained, but self-selected, mostly shown in figures without denominators, and with key methodological claims (the reliability of recognition, representativeness) resting on unpublished checks or cited studies. Citable for: DIMS identified on average about 30% of tablets by their logo, measurements and a colour test against a weekly list of recently analysed tablets; tablets resembling ecstasy, with similar logos, sometimes contained 2C-B or amphetamine instead; tablets sold as ecstasy often lacked MDMA around 1997 and 2009; LSD per unit varied from 1 to 500 µg; cocaine and speed purity and cutting agents as described. Not citable for: how reliable identification by logo is, how much tablets with the same logo vary, the composition of the whole Dutch market, or comparisons of the Netherlands with other countries.

key_findings.finding: Office testing: staff register a tablet's diameter, thickness, weight, colour, groove, speckling and logo (and its design), do a Marquis reagent test, and look the tablet up in an online database of tablets recently analysed in a laboratory, updated weekly. Because ecstasy tablets are usually made in large batches, a matching tablet is 'recognized', its average MDMA content and variation are taken as known, and it need not go to the laboratory. Laboratory results of recognized tablets that consumers still have analysed are used for validation, which the authors say has shown 99% reliability; on average 30% of tablets are determined this way. Tablets that are not recognized, or about which there is doubt, go to the laboratory.
key_findings.locator: Office testing, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column) and 2nd paragraph (right column)
key_findings.note: No data, period or definition of reliability are given for the 99% figure, and the variation said to be known for recognized tablets is not reported.

key_findings.finding: Editors' reading of Figure 3 (stacked areas, 300-dpi crop; approximate): tablets identified by recognition numbered about 4,300 in 1997 and about 4,600 in 2009, about 60–67% of all tablets in those years, against roughly 500 to 1,350 a year in 2002–2008 (about 20–37% of tablets).
key_findings.note: The paper gives no yearly numbers; values were obtained by subtracting the boundaries of stacked areas and may be off by a few hundred samples. The text's average of 30% (p. 622) does not state its period.

key_findings.finding: From two cited studies of people who use DIMS, the authors report that tablets are usually bought from a friend or a known dealer some time before a night out, and that knowing the dealer is considered far more important than getting tablets with a familiar logo or colour; the main reasons for testing were health concerns, curiosity about the results and circulated warnings.
key_findings.locator: Drugs users, 2nd paragraph (begun on p. 623; this part on p. 624, left column)

key_findings.finding: Look-alike tablets with other contents: in the second half of the 2000s 2C-B was frequently found in tablets sold as ecstasy that highly resembled ecstasy tablets, with similar logos, shapes and colours; amphetamine also appears in tablets with logos similar to ecstasy, although it is mostly sold as powder.
key_findings.locator: Speed, 4th paragraph (p. 627, left column); LSD and other hallucinogens, 4th paragraph (p. 629, right column)

key_findings.finding: Tablets sold as ecstasy (laboratory-analysed, 1993–2010): two periods in which many tablets contained other substances instead of or besides MDMA, around 1997 (amphetamines) and around 2009 (mCPP). At the low points only 30% of tablets handed in during October 1997 contained MDMA or an MDMA-like substance, and only 40% in March 2009 contained MDMA. MDEA and MDA, present in about 30% of tablets before 1997, virtually disappeared afterwards. New substances appeared around 1997 (MBDB, 2C-B, atropine, 4-MTA, PMA, the last followed by a national warning) and around 2009 (mCPP, mephedrone).
key_findings.note: The October 1997 and March 2009 values are monthly lows; Figure 5 shows years only, and no denominators are given.

key_findings.finding: Editors' reading of Figure 5 (300-dpi crop; approximate): MDMA as the only active substance in about 44% of tablets in 1997 and about 54% in 2009, about 85–88% in 2000–2004 and about 67% in 2010; in 2009 roughly a quarter of tablets contained no ecstasy-like substance at all.
MDMA content: between 1996 and 2001 less than half of ecstasy tablets contained more than 70 mg MDMA, as in 2009 (42%); before 1997 and between 2000 and 2009 more than half did.
key_findings.locator: Ecstasy, 4th paragraph (continued on p. 625, left column)
key_findings.note: The periods overlap (1996, 2000 and 2001 fall in both); see reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Speed: 8,239 powders bought as speed were handed in from 1992 to July 2010; about 85% contained enough amphetamine to quantify; in 1997–2001 over 20% did not (over 40% in 1999). Among powders with detectable amphetamine (1995–2010), mean purity was 30.2 ± 0.2% (mean ± SEM), below 20% from July 1998 to April 2001, below 5% in January 2000, and 18% at its low in December 2008; caffeine rose as amphetamine fell; 4-fluoroamphetamine and 4-methylamphetamine appeared during the 2008–2009 shortage.

Cocaine: on average 10% of powders sold as cocaine contained no quantifiable cocaine; the rest averaged 56 ± 0.3% (mean ± SEM), 66.3 ± 0.7% in 1993–1999 against 54.9 ± 0.8% in 2000–2010. About 10% contained a synthetic local anaesthetic (purity 44.6 ± 0.9% against 57.0 ± 0.3% without), and powders with other active adulterants averaged 38.8 ± 0.4% against 62.1 ± 0.3%. In Table 1 (titled 2005–2009) phenacetin was in 38% of samples, levamisole 21% (its mean ± SEM, 7.4 ± 0.3, n = 338, is footnoted 'Data from 2010'), caffeine 15%, lidocaine 8%, procaine 7%, diltiazem 6%, hydroxyzine 3%. Atropine, found in 2005 and 2007, was accompanied by hospitalizations and deaths in the Netherlands and across the border (Italy, France, Germany, Belgium).

LSD: samples sold as LSD rose from 6 in 1999 to a peak of 99 in 2003 (66 in the first half of 2010); around 80% contained LSD, except in 2002 (26%), when the rest held no quantifiable LSD or traces of other compounds such as methamphetamine or DOB; in 2007 some papertrips contained fentanyl, prompting a warning; the yearly average LSD per unit ranged from 20 to 96 µg, and single units from 1 to 500 µg.
key_findings.locator: LSD and other hallucinogens, 3rd paragraph; Figure 10

key_findings.finding: On representativeness, the authors cite two studies suggesting that people who use the testing services are broadly similar to people who do not, and treat DIMS's target group as a reasonable reflection of all people who use drugs recreationally; they also state that DIMS results are not an exact representation of the market and that a testing system reaches only a fraction of all people who use or may use drugs.
key_findings.locator: Drugs users, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (pp. 623–624); Discussion, 6th paragraph (p. 632)

key_findings.finding: International part (narrative, others' data): DanceSafe in the United States is described as working much like the DIMS recognition list, except that the consumer does the colour test and combines it with tablet characteristics on its website; Figure 11 (2004–2008, from EMCDDA and other reports) shows tablets containing MDMA-like substances, MDMA per tablet and powder purity in other countries, without Dutch data; because methods differ, the authors call the results indicative of trends rather than exact comparisons.
key_findings.locator: Other drug markets and monitors, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (p. 630); Figure 11 (p. 631)

reporting_issues.issue: The ecstasy text gives overlapping periods: fewer than 50% of tablets above 70 mg MDMA between 1996 and 2001, but more than 50% before 1997 and between 2000 and 2009, so 1996, 2000 and 2001 fall in both.
reporting_issues.consequence: The statements on tablets above 70 mg cannot be cited by year.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 11 is introduced as a comparison of other countries' monitoring results with those of DIMS (p. 630), but none of its four panels includes the Netherlands.
reporting_issues.consequence: No Dutch–international comparison is shown; the statement that amphetamine purity is considerably higher in the Netherlands compares Figure 7 with Figure 11 across different methods.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 (cocaine adulterants) is titled 2005–2009, but levamisole's mean ± SEM (7.4 ± 0.3, n = 338) carries the footnote 'Data from 2010'; whether its 21% share is also from 2010 is not stated. Atropine is listed as present in 0% of samples yet quantified in 5 samples (2.0 ± 3.0, mean ± SEM).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; part of the levamisole row refers to another year, and atropine's 0% is a rounded figure.

reporting_issues.issue: The text says that for a recognized tablet the average MDMA content and the variation are known, and that validation has shown 99% reliability of the recognition list (p. 622), but neither the variation nor the validation data are reported.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper gives no basis for claims about how much tablets with the same logo vary or how reliable identification by appearance is.

reporting_issues.issue: Figure 3's caption says 1992–2010, but its axis ends at 2009, and its category of samples 'not analyzed' is not explained (in the editors' reading it rises to roughly 2,000 samples in 2009).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; what happened to the samples counted as not analysed is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: A typical ecstasy tablet is said to contain 80–100 mg MDMA, without a source; the same group's laboratory data give lower yearly medians (Vogels et al., 2009, PDF p. 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: Do not cite this range as a DIMS finding.

reporting_issues.issue: The monthly lows for ecstasy (30% of tablets with MDMA or an MDMA-like substance in October 1997; 40% with MDMA in March 2009) are given without denominators or monthly data, and the yearly Figure 5 cannot confirm them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite them as the authors' statements, not as checked figures.

verification.source_read: PDF (version of record), Drug Testing and Analysis 3, 621–634: all pages (text pp. 621–632, references pp. 632–634); text extracted and every number checked on pages rendered at 110 dpi; Figures 3 and 5 read on 300-dpi crops (values marked approximate); Tables 1–2 checked on the rendered pages; Figures 4, 7, 9, 10 and 11 described from the rendered pages without extracting values; no supplement. No funding, acknowledgement or conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
